subtype: Approach: promising to start on Monday [Pitfall]
passage: Dear Rajni Masi, you asked how my plan to cut down my phone time is going. I'm embarrassed to say it hasn't started. Not truly. First I said I'd start after the festival. Then I said after the unit tests. Then Monday, because Mondays are for beginnings. Then the next Monday, because that Monday was a bad one. Each time the reason sounds good to me, and each time I check the report and the hours are the same, five or six a day. I can see that the better start date keeps moving, like the horizon. I keep making the promise because it feels good to make it. I'm writing to you so that it is on paper. Love, Pradeep

qa.q: What reasons did Pradeep give for postponing the plan?
qa.a: After the festival, after the unit tests, and next Monday.

qa.q: How does Pradeep feel writing to Rajni Masi?
qa.a: Embarrassed and a bit trapped: the promises feel good to make but nothing has changed.

qa.q: What could Pradeep do instead of waiting for a better date, and why?
qa.a: Start today with one small change, since waiting for a perfect start date is what keeps the habit going.

qa.q: How does the delay look to Rajni Masi?
qa.a: Rajni Masi sees repeated promises with no change, and may be worried but also relieved that Pradeep is being honest.

grounding: A teen keeps delaying a plan to a better start date, so the habit continues unchanged for months.

subtype: Approach: promising to start on Monday [Pitfall]
passage:
Baljeet, you want to know how my big phone plan is going? I'm Deepak, king of Mondays, so let me tell you.
In July I said I'd start after the unit tests, because why start during tests. After tests there was Raksha Bandhan and cousins visiting, so obviously after that. Then it was “first Monday of September”, a clean start. That Monday I had a cold. The next Monday there was a cricket match on at night, so not a fair week. Then Navratri. Then “after Diwali, properly”.
It's almost December. I've written the plan four times, in four notebooks. It's a good plan! Phone out of the room at night, a limit on videos. I just haven't done a single day of it.
And my screen time is the same as in July. Exactly the same.
So honestly, Baljeet, what if tonight is the Monday?

qa.q: How many times has Deepak written the plan?
How does Deepak seem to feel about all the delays?
qa.a: Deepak jokes about it but sounds frustrated and a bit ashamed that months passed with no change.

qa.q: What would you advise Deepak instead of waiting for a clean start?
qa.a: Start one small part of the plan tonight, like the phone out of the room, since any day works and the perfect start never comes.

qa.q: How might Baljeet see Deepak's string of Mondays?
qa.a: Baljeet may find it funny and familiar, but also see clearly that waiting for the right date has cost months.

grounding: Shows a teen pushing a screen plan to a better start date again and again, after tests, festivals and Mondays, so the habit stays unchanged for months.

subtype: Approach: promising to start on Monday [Pitfall]
passage:
I'm Ritu. I sit next to Pooja, and I've been hearing about her phone plan since June.
In June it was, “After the first unit test.” In July, “After my birthday, I'm not starting in my birthday week.” In August she showed me a timetable drawn with coloured pens: phone locked in a drawer from eight to ten, one hour of videos only. “From Monday.” That Monday there was a class trip, so, “Next Monday.”
September had the Ganesh festival. October had exams, “and you can't change habits during exams, everyone knows that.”
It's November. The timetable is still in her notebook; I saw it yesterday, a bit faded. Every morning she tells me what time she slept. Last night it was two.
I don't think she's lazy. I think she's waiting to feel ready. I don't know if that feeling ever comes.

qa.q: What time did Pooja sleep last night?
Why does Pooja keep pushing the start date?
qa.a: She seems to be waiting to feel ready, perhaps anxious that starting in a busy week would only fail.

qa.q: What could Pooja try instead of waiting for the right Monday?
qa.a: Pick the smallest piece of the timetable, like the drawer from eight to ten, and do it tonight, whatever the week holds.

qa.q: How does the delay look to Ritu?
qa.a: Ritu doesn't judge Pooja as lazy, but is quietly worried the right moment will never come while the late nights go on.

grounding: A classmate watches a teen push her screen plan to a better start date month after month, while the late nights continue unchanged.
